hook: A pilot's instruments show altitude on one dial and climb rate on another. An experienced pilot can glance at one and picture the other: when the altimeter peaks, the climb rate reads zero. Sketching $f'$ from $f$, and $f$ from $f'$, is the same skill, and the exam tests it with graphs every year.

prereq.q: If $f$ is concave up on an interval, then $f'$ is
At a relative maximum of a differentiable $f$, $f'$

figure.caption: Line the two graphs up: where $f$ peaks or bottoms out, $f'$ crosses zero; where $f$ inflects, $f'$ turns; where $f$ rises, $f'$ is above the axis.

chain.effect: the graph of $f'$ is above (below) the $x$-axis there

chain.cause: $f$ has a peak or valley with a flat tangent line
chain.effect: the graph of $f'$ crosses the $x$-axis there
the graph of $f'$ has a peak or valley there
the graph of $f'$ jumps, with no value at that point

ideas: Read a graph of $f$ for features, not values: where it rises, falls, peaks, bends. Each feature becomes a feature of the graph of the derivative.
$f$ (sign of slope) $\to$ $f'$ (sign of value). $f$ (concavity) $\to$ $f'$ (rising or falling). Inflection of $f$ $\to$ peak or valley of $f'$.
Going the other way, from $f'$ to $f$: zeros of $f'$ where its sign changes are extrema of $f$; turns of $f'$ are inflection points of $f$; a constant $f'$ means $f$ is a straight line.
The same pattern links $f'$ and $f''$: the slope of the graph of $f'$ is $f''$.

misconception.wrong: The graph of $f'$ looks like the graph of $f$, shifted or flattened.
misconception.right: $f'$ records slopes, not heights. A peak of $f$ is a zero of $f'$, and a peak of $f'$ is the steepest point of $f$, an inflection point. Build the sketch feature by feature: signs first, then where $f'$ rises or falls.

summary: Sketch a derivative feature by feature: where $f$ rises, $f'$ is positive; where $f$ is flat at a peak or valley, $f'$ crosses zero; where $f$ is concave up, $f'$ rises; where $f$ inflects, $f'$ turns; where $f$ has a corner, $f'$ jumps. Read the same links backward to sketch $f$ from $f'$.
